fetched_contents.text: Sulfate Soundness Test of Aggregates, Estimating Durability Why the Soundness Test of Aggregate is Performed Construction aggregates resistant to degradation from freeze-thaw and weathering actions are likely to perform better over the long term in concrete and asphalt mixes for paving applications. These materials typically feature good overall durability and have low void ratios and low absorption rates, as noted in a previous blog Aggregate Properties You Need To Know: Strength and Durability. Significant quality variability in aggregates sourced from natural deposits and formations calls for care in the production and selection of materials, particularly in areas subject to freeze-thaw cycles. Historical service records of the specific aggregate type are a valuable resource. Lacking these, sulfate soundness testing outlined in ASTM C88 or AASHTO T 104 provides a valid preliminary estimate of freeze-thaw and weathering resistance. What is Sulfate Soundness? Procedures for this popular test method are straightforward, and the equipment required is neither sophisticated nor expensive. Meaningful results are produced in a reasonable time compared to other methods. The statistical precision of this test method is not high, and there will be variation between outcomes using the sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate solutions. Test results should be considered a preliminary estimate of aggregate suitability and not used for outright rejection of the source. Close control over testing elements like temperature, timing, types of containers, and sieving methods will minimize variability. When needed, results can be confirmed with other tests. AASHTO T 103 uses similar procedures but requires many more cycles in extreme freezing and thawing temperatures. Sodium chloride, alcohol, or water immersion solutions are used instead of sulfates. ASTM C666 tests samples of concrete mixes in air or water using freeze-thaw cycles. Summary of the Sulfate Soundness Test Separated size fractions of the fine and coarse aggregate sample are immersed for timed cycles into a sodium sulfate (Na2SO4) or magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) solution, then oven-dried and immersed again. Crystals of the salt solution grow in voids and fissures of the aggregate particles during the immersion and drying cycles, simulating the expansive force of ice crystals and causing degradation of the particles. After completion of the test cycles and a final washing, each size fraction is again sieved and weighed to determine the percentage of mass lost by degradation during the process. A qualitative examination of the coarse aggregate classifies the degree of damage sustained by the particles. Test results between the sodium and magnesium solutions do not correlate. Sulfate Solution Preparation Chemicals used for the soundness test of aggregates include Sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate USP grade salts. These are widely available from chemical suppliers in either anhydrous or crystalline form. To prepare the immersion fluid, stir the chemical salts in 25° to 30°C (77° to 86°F) water until the mixture is saturated and some solids precipitate back out of solution. About 350g of anhydrous or 750g of crystalline chemical per liter of water is usually sufficient. The solution volume must be at least five times the volume of the solids of the samples to be immersed at one time. The prepared mixture must be covered to reduce evaporation, frequently stirred to break up the salt cake, and maintained at 70±2°F (21±1°C) for 48 hours before use. In some cases, like a temperature-controlled laboratory, the temperature limitations are easily met. Other situations require that the solution be artificially heated or cooled to maintain compliance. At the time of use, caked material must be broken up and stirred back into solution. The specific gravity of the solution must be between 1.151 and 1.174 for sodium sulfate or between 1.295 and 1.308 for magnesium sulfate. Aggregate Sample Preparation Selection and preparation of the aggregate sample fractions must strictly follow the procedures in the ASTM or AASHTO standard test methods. The bulk samples are thoroughly washed over specified sieves and oven-dried before separating into the specified size fractions. * For fine aggregates, test portions consist of 100g of material from each specified sieve fraction. * Coarse aggregate specimens consist of particle size groups and may combine specified amounts of two size fractions to make up their total mass. Performing the Sulfate Soundness Test Record the initial mass of each fraction and immerse the samples in the prepared solution for 16 to 18 hours. The containers are covered to prevent evaporation or contamination, and temperature is maintained and recorded at 70±2°F (21±1°C). At the end of each immersion cycle, the sample is drained, oven-dried to a constant mass, and cooled to room temperature before immersion for the next cycle. Each cycle takes about one day, and five cycles are typically required. Once the cycles are complete, the sample is washed with a reverse flow of warm water. The final wash water is tested with a barium chloride solution to ensure the sample is entirely free of the sulfate solution. The barium solution will turn cloudy if sulfates are present. Each fraction is dried and sieved again, and the percent loss from the initial gradation is calculated. A qualitative examination is also performed on fractions coarser than 3/4in (19.0mm). Particles from these fractions are grouped according to the type of degradation like splitting, flaking, cracking, disintegration, etc. Particles from each group are counted and recorded. F. da Costa 1,2,3,* 1 Programa de Pós-Graduação em Engenharia Ambiental, Instituto Federal Fluminense, Macaé 27932-050, RJ, Brazil 2 Instituto Politécnico, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Macaé 27930-560, RJ, Brazil 3 Programa de Pós-Graduação em Engenharia Ambiental, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro 21941-909, RJ, Brazil Author to whom correspondence should be addressed. Submission received: 18 June 2025 / Revised: 30 July 2025 / Accepted: 8 August 2025 / Published: 14 August 2025 Abstract The construction industry is responsible for 50% of mineral resource extraction and 35% of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. In this context, concrete stands out as one of the most consumed materials in the world. More than 30 billion tons of this material are produced annually, resulting in the extraction of around 19.4 billion tons of aggregates (mainly sand and gravel) per year. Therefore, it is urgent to develop strategies that aim to minimize the environmental impacts arising from this production chain. Currently, one of the most widely adopted solutions is the production of concrete through the reuse of construction and demolition waste. Thus, the objective of this research is to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) on the use of recycled aggregates in concrete production, aiming to increase urban resilience by reducing the consumption of natural aggregates. An extensive search was performed in one of the most respected scientific databases (Scopus), and after a careful selection process, the main articles related to the topic were considered eligible through the PRISMA protocol. The selected manuscripts were then subjected to bibliographic and bibliometric analyses, allowing us to reach the state-of-the-art on the subject. The results obtained on the replacement rates of natural aggregate by recycled aggregate indicate that the recommendations vary from 20 to 60%, and these rates may be higher as long as the recycled aggregate is characterized, and may reach up to 100% as long as the matric concrete has a minimum compressive strength of 60 MPa. The specific gravity of most recycled aggregates ranges from 1.91 to 2.70, maintaining an average density of 2.32 g/cm3. Residual mortar adhered to recycled aggregates ranges from 20 to 56%. The water absorption process of recycled aggregate can vary from 2 to 15%. The mechanical strength of mixtures with recycled aggregates is significantly reduced due to the amount of mortar adhered to the aggregates. The use of recycled aggregates results in a compressive strength approximately 2.6 to 43% lower than that of concrete with natural aggregates, depending on the replacement rate. The same behavior was identified in relation to tensile strength. The modulus of elasticity showed a reduction of 25%, and the flexural strength was reduced by up to 15%. 1. The sulphate soundness test measures an aggregate’s resistance to disintegration by weathering and, in particular, freeze-thaw cycles, while also providing a preliminary estimate of its resistance to sulfate attack [N1-R2][N2-R2]. The test’s physical and chemical basis is that sulfate solutions can cause expansion and degradation in aggregate particles, especially in voids and fissures, by forming crystals that simulate ice expansion and thereby degrade the particles over repeated cycles [N1-F1]. The test procedure described in the evidence is straightforward: aggregate samples are separated into size fractions, immersed in a sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄) or magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) solution for timed cycles, oven-dried, re-immersed, and repeated for a total of five cycles, followed by washing and final weighing to determine mass loss [N1-F1]. The test also includes a qualitative examination of coarse aggregate for damage types such as splitting, flaking, cracking, and disintegration, which helps interpret the degree of degradation [N1-F1].

The test is interpreted by comparing the measured soundness loss or expansion against thresholds and reporting conventions. The evidence emphasizes that the statistical precision of the test method is not high, and results can vary between sodium sulfate and magnesium sulfate solutions [N1-F1]. It also notes that the test results should be considered a preliminary estimate of aggregate suitability rather than an outright rejection criterion, and that close control of testing conditions such as temperature, timing, and sieving can minimize variability [N1-F1]. The standards referenced in the evidence include ASTM C88 and AASHTO T 104 for sulfate soundness testing, with ASTM C88 or AASHTO T 104 described as providing a valid preliminary estimate of freeze-thaw and weathering resistance [N1-R1][N2-R1]. The test is also compared with AASHTO T 103, which uses similar procedures but requires more cycles in extreme freezing and thawing conditions and uses different immersion solutions [N1-F1]. Overall, the test is intended to estimate durability and long-term performance under environmental exposure, not to provide a definitive, highly precise measure [N1-F1].

## How sulphate soundness test results affect the assessment of recycled aggregates' suitability for unbound pavement applications

Sulphate soundness test results are an important but partial piece of evidence in assessing whether recycled aggregates are suitable for unbound pavement applications. The test is designed to estimate an aggregate’s resistance to disintegration by weathering and, in particular, freeze-thaw cycles, while also providing a preliminary estimate of its resistance to sulfate attack [N1-R2][N2-R2]. In practical terms, the test measures how much an aggregate degrades under repeated exposure to sulfate solutions, with the degradation mechanism involving salt crystal growth in voids and fissures, simulating the expansive force of ice and causing particle breakdown [N1-F1]. The procedure is standardized and repeatable, but the evidence also notes that the statistical precision of the test method is not high and that results can vary between sodium sulfate and magnesium sulfate solutions [N1-F1]. It is therefore best treated as a preliminary estimate rather than a definitive rejection criterion [N1-F1].

### 1. What sulphate soundness actually tells us, and how it is interpreted

The test procedure separates aggregate samples into size fractions, immerses them in sodium sulfate or magnesium sulfate solution for timed cycles, oven-dries, re-immerses, and repeats for a total of five cycles, then washes and weighs them to determine mass loss [N1-F1]. It also includes a qualitative examination of coarse aggregate for damage types such as splitting, flaking, cracking, and disintegration [N1-F1]. The standards referenced in the evidence are ASTM C88 and AASHTO T 104, both described as providing a valid preliminary estimate of freeze-thaw and weathering resistance [N1-R1][N2-R1]. The test can also be compared with AASHTO T 103, which uses similar procedures but requires more cycles in extreme freezing and thawing conditions and uses different immersion solutions [N1-F1].

The interpretation of the results is therefore tied to thresholds and reporting conventions. Because the test results should be considered a preliminary estimate rather than an outright rejection criterion, the evidence suggests that close control of testing conditions is necessary to minimize variability [N1-F1]. In other words, sulphate soundness provides a relative durability indication, not a precise pass/fail score, and the result must be interpreted cautiously alongside other tests [N1-F1].

### 2. How sulphate soundness results influence pavement performance and design

The evidence links poor aggregate quality to pavement distress modes such as disintegration, ravelling, cracking, bleeding, instability, rutting, and deformation [N5-R2]. For unbound pavements, the durability and soundness of the aggregate material are especially relevant because poor quality can lead to cracking and disintegration that compromise the layer’s structural integrity [N1-R2][N2-R2]. The evidence further shows that sulphate soundness is connected to broader pavement performance concerns, including rutting and cracking requirements, and that pavement design often balances these competing distress modes [N5-R1][N5-R3].

In the broader pavement design picture, the durability of the aggregate is part of the layered behavior of the pavement system and affects how the aggregate interacts with surrounding materials [N5-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that pavement performance is influenced by the interaction between materials and by the layered behavior of the pavement system, with cracking and rutting being performance criteria that must be balanced in mixture design [N5-R1][N5-R3]. This means that poor sulphate soundness can reduce the aggregate’s ability to resist expansion and degradation, which may translate into more cracking, instability, and rutting over time [N5-R2].

As for design margins or safety factors, the evidence does not provide explicit numerical margins, but it does support the use of a conservative interpretation approach. The test results should not be used for outright rejection, and close control of testing conditions is needed to minimize variability [N1-F1]. In broader pavement design, the evidence supports performance-based approaches that balance rutting and cracking requirements, with design guidelines and mixture testing used to achieve acceptable performance [N5-R1][N5-R3]. So, the practical implication is that sulphate soundness results are treated as part of the performance assessment, not as a standalone rejection criterion [N1-F1][N5-R2].

In other words, recycling can introduce variability and potentially increase susceptibility to sulfate attack, but the exact effect depends on the specific recycling process and the resulting material properties [N3-F2][N3-R3].

The test procedure described in the evidence is straightforward: aggregate samples are separated into size fractions, immersed in a sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄) or magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) solution for timed cycles, oven-dried, re-immersed, and repeated for a total of five cycles, followed by washing and final weighing to determine mass loss [N1-F1]. The test also includes a qualitative examination of coarse aggregate for damage types such as splitting, flaking, cracking, and disintegration, which helps interpret the degree of degradation [N1-F1].

The test is interpreted by comparing the measured soundness loss or expansion against thresholds and reporting conventions. The evidence emphasizes that the statistical precision of the test method is not high, and results can vary between sodium sulfate and magnesium sulfate solutions [N1-F1]. It also notes that the test results should be considered a preliminary estimate of aggregate suitability rather than an outright rejection criterion, and that close control of testing conditions such as temperature, timing, and sieving can minimize variability [N1-F1]. The test is also compared with AASHTO T 103, which uses similar procedures but requires more cycles in extreme freezing and thawing conditions and uses different immersion solutions [N1-F1]. The test also includes a qualitative examination of coarse aggregate for damage types such as splitting, flaking, cracking, and disintegration, which helps interpret the degree of degradation [N1-F1].

It also notes that the test results should be considered a preliminary estimate of aggregate suitability rather than an outright rejection criterion, and that close control of testing conditions such as temperature, timing, and sieving can minimize variability [N1-F1].
